title: Interference of light — Young's double slit experiment
topicTitle: Interference of light — Young's double slit experiment
notes: Young's experiment lets one wavefront illuminate two narrow slits. The two waves that leave the slits stay in step, so they interfere on a distant screen. Two separate lamps do not keep that fixed phase.
Where the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths, the waves arrive in phase and the fringe is bright. Where the path difference is an odd number of half wavelengths, the fringe is dark.

The central fringe is bright because the two paths are equal. The bright fringes are equally spaced. The spacing is β = λ D / d, with D the screen distance and d the slit separation, when D is much larger than d.
A longer wavelength, a more distant screen, or closer slits all widen the pattern. Closing one slit removes the two-source fringes and leaves the single-slit spread.
White light gives a white central fringe and coloured fringes farther out, because each colour has its own spacing. The red fringes sit farther apart than the blue ones.
The path difference at a small angle is d sinθ, or d x / D on the screen. Setting that equal to m λ locates the bright fringe of order m.
